items.title: Eric Alexander interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 31, 2010
items.q: you’re on the bandstand and, you know, Louis Hayes is playing 300 miles an hour on the drums and Harold is playing piano.

ctx.x: It’s definitely bad in some ways. I mean one of the most obvious ways that it’s bad that is painfully obvious to me, if I give one kid “Charlie Parker with Strings,” and say this is the only thing you’re allowed to listen for six months. I want you to learn every note that he plays on at least two or three of these tunes. And then another guy I give a 30 gigabyte iPod and say “have fun.” I guarantee the guy with the one record is going to come out

better. He’s going to learn more. There’s no question. Because playing this music is about knowing, it’s not how much you know but it’s how well you know what you supposedly know. If you have a little bit of information that you have absolutely mastered, you’re going to play better than somebody with kind of a vague understanding of a lot of things. Because in order to be effective as an improviser you have to be able to — it’s not like somebody who could pass a test. You know there are people all over the United…

I couldn’t agree more. What experiences have you had perhaps with Charles Earland or some of the other fellows that you were a sideman with that impacted your eventual role as a leader. Did you learn stuff from those guys musically and otherwise that helped you out?
